goldenPoints: Epidural haematoma: biconvex (lentiform) collection that does not cross sutures; lucid interval.
Subdural haematoma: crescent-shaped collection that crosses sutures, from bridging veins.
Empty delta sign on CT venography = cerebral venous sinus thrombosis.
Double bubble sign in a neonate = duodenal atresia.
Bird-beak / rat-tail oesophagus on barium = achalasia cardia.
Apple-core lesion of the colon = carcinoma; string sign of Kantor = Crohn disease.
Raindrop skull / punched-out lesions + CRAB features = multiple myeloma.
FDG (F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose) is the isotope of PET; Ga-68 PSMA PET is for prostate cancer.
Most radiosensitive tissue: bone marrow / lymphoid tissue; least sensitive: mature neurons / muscle.
Lead apron for radiation protection is 0.5 mm lead equivalent.
intro: Radiology carries 10 questions in every FMGE paper (radiodiagnosis plus radiotherapy). The stems are dominated by named signs and classic image descriptions: intracranial bleeds on CT, bowel signs on plain films and barium, skull lesions, PET isotopes and radiation-protection facts. These 10 topics collect the descriptions you must recognise in words, since the paper tests the picture through its story.

branches.label: Chest X-ray
leaves: Right middle lobe silhouettes heart border

subject: Radiology
tagline: Named signs, investigation of choice and image descriptions in words — radiology is a vocabulary test.

topics.askedAs: Lucid interval / biconvex bleed on CT
topics.oneLiner: Biconvex = epidural; crescent = subdural; blood in cisterns = subarachnoid.
points: Epidural haematoma: biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection; limited by sutures, can cross the midline venous sinuses
Classic story: head injury, brief unconsciousness, lucid interval, then rapid deterioration — middle meningeal artery bleed
Subdural haematoma: crescent-shaped collection that crosses sutures but not the midline; torn bridging veins
Chronic subdural: elderly/alcoholic, fluctuating confusion after trivial trauma weeks earlier
Subarachnoid haemorrhage: thunderclap headache; blood fills the basal cisterns and sulci; aneurysm is the usual cause
Diffuse axonal injury: multiple small spotty haemorrhages at grey–white junction with basal cisterns preserved/full
Empty delta sign on contrast CT/MR venography: cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Depressed skull fracture from a focal blow (hammer): CT shows the depressed fragment — 'pond' fracture in infants
Investigation of choice for acute head injury: non-contrast CT head
topics.title: Intracranial Haemorrhage on CT
topics.trap: Epidural is limited by SUTURES; subdural is limited by dural reflections (falx/tentorium) — examiners swap these.

topics.askedAs: White-out / silhouette sign / meniscus — name the lesion
topics.oneLiner: Trachea pushed away + white-out = effusion or pneumothorax; pulled towards = collapse/fibrosis.
points: Total white-out with trachea shifted AWAY: massive pleural effusion (or tension pneumothorax if hyperresonant story)
White-out with trachea pulled TOWARDS the side: collapse / post-pneumonectomy / fibrosis
Silhouette sign: loss of a border means disease in the lobe touching it — right heart border lost = right middle lobe
Pleural effusion: blunting of costophrenic angle with a meniscus sign (higher laterally) on the erect film
Pericardial effusion: globular 'water-bottle / flask' heart, muffled sounds, Beck-type picture
Cannonball secondaries in the lungs: metastases (renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, testis)
Sand-mine / silica worker with nodular opacities: silicosis — eggshell calcification of hilar nodes is classic
Tension pneumothorax: hyperinflated black hemithorax, mediastinum pushed away, flattened diaphragm
Investigation of choice for pulmonary embolism: CT pulmonary angiography
topics.title: Chest X-Ray: Classic Patterns
topics.trap: A white lung with the trachea pushed away is fluid/air under pressure — never collapse.

topics.askedAs: Barium picture described — name the diagnosis
topics.oneLiner: Beak = achalasia, apple-core = cancer, string = Crohn, corkscrew = spasm.
points: Achalasia cardia: smooth 'bird-beak / rat-tail' tapering of the lower oesophagus with a dilated oesophagus above
Carcinoma oesophagus: irregular, shouldered, apple-core-like narrowing with mucosal destruction
Diffuse oesophageal spasm: corkscrew / rosary-bead oesophagus on barium swallow
Zenker diverticulum: outpouching at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction (Killian dehiscence)
Colon carcinoma: apple-core lesion — short, irregular stricture with overhanging edges
Crohn disease of terminal ileum: string sign of Kantor — thin stream of barium through a narrowed segment
Ulcerative colitis: loss of haustra, lead-pipe colon; toxic megacolon is the feared complication
Sigmoid diverticulosis on barium enema: multiple small rounded outpouchings (saw-tooth colon)
Hirschsprung disease: narrow aganglionic distal segment with a dilated proximal colon (transition zone)
topics.title: GI Radiology: Barium Signs
topics.trap: Smooth tapering = benign/achalasia; irregular shouldered narrowing = malignancy — the margins decide.

topics.oneLiner: Double bubble = duodenum blocked; coffee bean = sigmoid volvulus; free gas = perforation.
points: Duodenal atresia: double-bubble sign — gas in stomach and duodenal cap, none beyond; bilious vomiting in a newborn
Down syndrome is associated with duodenal atresia (and annular pancreas gives the same picture)
Pyloric stenosis: single large gastric bubble, string sign on contrast, olive mass clinically
Sigmoid volvulus: huge dilated loop rising from the pelvis — coffee-bean / bent-inner-tube sign
Caecal volvulus: comma-shaped dilated caecum displaced to the left upper quadrant
Free gas under the diaphragm on an erect chest film: hollow viscus perforation (e.g. NSAID-related peptic perforation)
Small-bowel obstruction: multiple central air-fluid levels, valvulae conniventes crossing the full width
Large-bowel obstruction: peripheral dilatation with haustral folds that do not cross fully
Intussusception: target/donut sign on ultrasound; air enema is both diagnostic and therapeutic
topics.title: Abdominal X-Ray Signs
topics.trap: Valvulae conniventes cross the whole lumen (small bowel); haustra do not (large bowel).

topics.oneLiner: Raindrop skull + back pain + anaemia in an older adult = myeloma until disproved.
points: Multiple myeloma: multiple punched-out lytic skull lesions — 'raindrop skull'
Myeloma bone lesions are purely lytic, so a bone scan may be cold/normal — skeletal survey is preferred
Lytic metastases: breast, lung, kidney, thyroid; sclerotic (osteoblastic) metastases: prostate
Superscan on bone scan: diffusely increased uptake with faint kidneys — widespread metastases (prostate) or metabolic bone disease
Angiomyolipoma of kidney: CT shows fat density within the renal mass — the fat is diagnostic
Bamboo spine: ankylosing spondylitis — squaring of vertebrae with syndesmophytes; HLA-B27 linked
Soap-bubble lesion at the epiphysis of a young adult: giant cell tumour (osteoclastoma)
Sunray spiculation with Codman triangle: osteosarcoma; onion-peel periosteal reaction: Ewing sarcoma
Painless hard metaphyseal mass in an adolescent: osteochondroma (exostosis) is the commonest benign bone tumour
topics.title: Bone & Skull Radiology
topics.trap: Myeloma is the lytic-lesion exception where the bone scan underperforms — choose skeletal survey.

topics.askedAs: Which scan for which tumour — isotope matching
topics.oneLiner: FDG for PET, PSMA for prostate, MIBG/DOTATATE for neuroendocrine tumours.
points: PET scan uses F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) — taken up by metabolically active cancer cells
Ga-68 PSMA PET-CT: investigation of choice for staging/biochemical recurrence of prostate cancer
Ga-68 DOTATATE PET: most sensitive imaging for well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours
MIBG scan: localises extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma / paraganglioma
Most commonly used radioisotope in diagnostic nuclear medicine overall: Technetium-99m
Renal perfusion / renal artery stenosis assessment: DTPA or MAG3 renogram (capoten renogram historically)
Vein of Galen malformation in a neonate with heart failure: midline hypoechoic lesion with bruit on cranial ultrasound
Horseshoe kidney and crossed fused ectopia are classic IVP/CT urogram descriptions
Investigation shown for the urinary tract with contrast in ureters and bladder: intravenous pyelogram (IVP/IVU)
topics.title: Nuclear Medicine & Investigation of Choice
topics.trap: PSMA = prostate; DOTATATE = neuroendocrine — stems swap the tracers between the two cancers.

topics.oneLiner: Cobalt-60 shoots gamma rays; a LINAC makes X-rays and electrons; 2 Gy a day is conventional.
points: Teletherapy (external beam) classic source: Cobalt-60, which emits gamma rays
Linear accelerator (LINAC) produces high-energy X-rays (photons) and electron beams — not gamma from a source
Conventional fractionation: 1.8–2 Gy per fraction, once daily, 5 days a week, over 6–8 weeks
Radiotherapy works mainly by causing DNA double-strand breaks in dividing cells
Most radiosensitive tissues: bone marrow, lymphoid tissue, gonads, intestinal crypt cells
Least radiosensitive: mature neurons and muscle — terminally differentiated cells resist radiation
Lymphocytes are the most radiosensitive blood cells; neurons among the least sensitive cells overall
Radiation pneumonitis can follow thoracic radiotherapy (e.g. after breast cancer treatment) weeks to months later
Brachytherapy: radioactive source placed in or next to the tumour (e.g. cervix)
topics.title: Radiotherapy Principles
topics.trap: A LINAC does not contain cobalt — 'which isotope in teletherapy' (Co-60) and 'what a LINAC produces' (X-rays) are different questions.

topics.askedAs: Lead apron thickness / most sensitive tissue
topics.oneLiner: 0.5 mm lead, marrow is most sensitive, distance and shielding protect.
points: Lead apron for personnel: 0.5 mm lead equivalent thickness is the standard answer
Most radiosensitive organ system: the haematopoietic (bone marrow) system; gonads are also highly sensitive
Radiation protection triad: minimise time, maximise distance, use shielding
Inverse square law: doubling the distance quarters the dose
ALARA principle: keep exposure As Low As Reasonably Achievable
Deterministic effects have a threshold (skin burns, cataract); stochastic effects (cancer) have no safe threshold
Pregnancy: the fetus is most vulnerable during organogenesis (roughly weeks 2–8/early first trimester)
Annual dose limits and personnel monitoring use film badges / TLD dosimeters
Lead glass screens and thyroid collars protect during fluoroscopy
topics.title: Radiation Protection & Biology
topics.trap: 'Most radiosensitive cell' (lymphocyte) vs 'least radiosensitive' (neuron) — stems ask both directions.

topics.oneLiner: Water's shows the maxillary antrum; Caldwell shows the frontal sinus.
points: Water's view (occipitomental): best for the maxillary sinuses
Caldwell view (occipitofrontal): best for the frontal sinuses and ethmoids
Frontal sinuses become visible on X-ray by about 6 years of age (pneumatise late)
Submentovertex view: sphenoid sinus and base of skull
Obliteration of the right cardiac border on CXR localises disease to the right middle lobe (silhouette logic)
On an abdominal CT, pancreas lies anterior to the splenic vein, between liver (right) and spleen (left)
Central venous catheter tip position is confirmed by chest X-ray (tip at the SVC–right atrium junction)
MRI field strength is measured in Tesla; most clinical scanners are 1.5 T or 3 T
CT numbers are expressed in Hounsfield units: water 0, air −1000, bone strongly positive
topics.title: Views, Sinuses & Imaging Basics
topics.trap: Water's = maxillary, Caldwell = frontal — the pair is asked almost every cycle.

topics.askedAs: Rapid dementia + myoclonus / pulsatile neck swelling
topics.oneLiner: Pattern-recognition stems reward the classic pairing: CJD, carotid body tumour, pericardial effusion.
points: Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, ataxia and visual disturbance: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease — MRI shows basal ganglia/cortical hyperintensity
Pulsatile swelling below the angle of the jaw with expansile impulse: carotid body tumour / carotid aneurysm territory — image with Doppler/CT angiography
Chest pain worse lying flat, better sitting up, muffled heart sounds: pericardial effusion — echocardiography is the investigation of choice
Charcot (neuropathic) knee in diabetes: swollen, deformed joint with surprisingly little pain
Perthes disease: limping 4–8-year-old boy — avascular necrosis of the femoral head; frog-leg lateral view helps
Renal angiomyolipoma bleeds (Wunderlich syndrome) — fat density on CT is the giveaway
Subarachnoid blood with a normal early CT does not exclude SAH — lumbar puncture for xanthochromia is the classic next step
In head injury with GCS 10 after a road accident: NCCT head is the first investigation
Post-tuberculosis hemoptysis with a cavity and intracavitary mass: aspergilloma — Monod sign (air crescent)
topics.title: Clinical Pattern Stems in Radiology
topics.trap: Monod sign (aspergilloma, mass inside an old cavity) differs from the air-crescent of invasive aspergillosis recovering from neutropenia.
